295.title: Pentecostals and charismatics
295.hook: Azusa Street, 1906: the fastest-growing Christians today, praying with gifts of the Spirit
295.howItsDone: Pentecostal and charismatic worship is often long and lively, with raised hands, spontaneous prayer, praying in tongues, and prayer for healing, while many charismatics also worship within Catholic, Anglican and other churches.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Methodists: John Wesley's heart, strangely warmed on Aldersgate Street. Your line was strangely warmed.

Los Angeles, April 1906. A run-down building on Azusa Street, once a church, lately a stable and a storeroom. Sawdust on the floor. Planks across nail kegs for benches. The preacher is William Seymour, a Black man, the son of formerly enslaved parents, blind in one eye. Night after night, people crowd in: Black and white, Mexican, Asian, rich and poor, side by side, in an America where that almost never happened. They pray for hours. Some weep, some shout, some fall silent, and some begin praying in languages they don't know. Newspapers mock them. Visitors come from across the world and go home changed. That dusty room became one of the main sparks of one of the largest movements in Christian history.
screen: `AZUSA STREET, 1906.` → `SAWDUST AND PLANKS.` → `SIDE BY SIDE, PRAYING FOR HOURS.`

segments.voice: Pentecostals take their name from Pentecost, the day in Acts 2 when the Holy Spirit came on the first disciples: "And they were all filled with the Holy Ghost, and began to speak with other tongues, as the Spirit gave them utterance." Pentecostals believe the same Spirit still gives the same gifts today: speaking in tongues, healing, prophecy, a word of wisdom. Paul lists these gifts in First Corinthians 12 and calls them charismata, gifts of grace. That's where charismatic comes from. Pentecostals belong to churches born from this movement, like the Assemblies of God or the Church of God in Christ. Charismatics are Christians in other churches, Catholic, Anglican, Lutheran, Baptist, who from the 1960s on began praying this way too, while staying in their own churches. Together they may be something like a quarter of all Christians on earth, most of them in Africa, Latin America and Asia. Their worship is often loud, joyful and long, with hands raised, and a strong sense that God is close and acting now. Others see it differently: some believe certain gifts, like tongues, ended with the apostles; many welcome the gifts but pray more quietly. The churches hold that disagreement openly. And a sad footnote to Azusa: within a few years, many Pentecostal churches divided along racial lines, like the rest of America. But one short prayer is shared by nearly every church: a medieval Latin hymn, Veni Sancte Spiritus, begins, come, Holy Spirit.
screen: `PENTECOST: THE SPIRIT COMES.` · `CHARISMATA: GIFTS OF GRACE.` · `PENTECOSTALS AND CHARISMATICS.` · `A QUARTER OF ALL CHRISTIANS?` · then, large: `AS THE SPIRIT GAVE THEM UTTERANCE.`

segments.voice: Rest your hands on your knees, palms up, and notice the difference from clenched hands: open hands can't grab or hold on; they can only receive. If you pray, say three words slowly on the breath, come, Holy Spirit, then wait, without asking for anything in particular. If you don't pray, just sit with your hands open, ready for whatever the day gives.
Charismata. Paul's word for gifts of grace in Greek, the root of charismatic: a gift the Spirit still gives today.
Your line: come, holy spirit. Gifts of grace, still given. Day two hundred ninety-five, done.

296.title: What they share
296.hook: the creeds, baptism, the Lord's Prayer, and one Lord; many now pray together
296.howItsDone: Many churches keep the Week of Prayer for Christian Unity each January, often with services where members of different churches pray together, and many young Christians travel to Taizé to worship side by side.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was charismata, from a dusty room on Azusa Street. Your line was come, holy spirit.

On a hill in the French countryside sits a village called Taizé. Young people arrive from all over the world with backpacks and sleeping bags: Catholics, Lutherans, Orthodox, Anglicans, Pentecostals, people with no church at all. Three times a day a bell rings, and everyone walks into a long, low, candlelit church and sits on the floor. They sing short, simple songs, over and over, in many languages. Then a long silence, together. Nobody asks which church you belong to. Brother Roger, a young Swiss man who took in refugees during the war, started it in 1940. After two weeks of splits, today's word is the long work of coming back together.
screen: `A VILLAGE CALLED TAIZÉ.` → `EVERY CHURCH, ON ONE FLOOR.` → `SINGING, THEN SILENCE.`

segments.voice: Ecumenism comes from the Greek oikoumene, the whole inhabited world. The early church's councils were called ecumenical because they gathered bishops from everywhere. Now it means the movement to heal divisions between churches. Its heart is a prayer Jesus prays in John's Gospel, the night before he dies: "That they all may be one; as thou, Father, art in me, and I in thee." For long stretches, the churches didn't pray that together. In the twentieth century, that began to change. A missionary conference in Edinburgh in 1910 found that division confused the very people they hoped to reach. The World Council of Churches, founded in 1948, now brings together Orthodox, Anglican and Protestant churches worldwide. The Catholic Church isn't a member, but since the Second Vatican Council it has worked closely alongside, calling other Christians separated brothers and sisters. Many evangelical and Pentecostal churches keep their distance from formal bodies, but pray with other Christians in their own ways. The differences are real, and nobody pretends otherwise: communion, authority, ministry. But much is shared. The Bible. The Nicene Creed, said in many churches. The Lord's Prayer. Baptism in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, which many churches now recognize in each other. And one Lord. Every January there's a Week of Prayer for Christian Unity. Now look back: one church, then many; the councils; the ancient churches of the east; the Church of the East; 1054; the Orthodox; the Catholics; the Reformation; Lutherans and the Reformed; Anglicans; Anabaptists; Baptists; Methodists; Pentecostals. Fifteen days, one family.

If you don't pray, just picture them all, saying the same words in many languages.

297.title: I believe
297.hook: a creed from credo, I believe: a short summary said together for centuries
297.howItsDone: Many churches say the Apostles' Creed at baptisms and at morning and evening prayer, and the Nicene Creed at the main Sunday service, with the whole congregation speaking together.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was ecumenism, and a village called Taizé. Your line was that they may be one.

Rome, around the year 200, as an early church handbook describes it. It's the night before Easter, and a woman stands waist-deep in water, about to be baptized. She's spent months, maybe years, learning. Now the bishop asks her three questions. Do you believe in God the Father Almighty? I believe, she says, and she goes under the water. Do you believe in Christ Jesus, the Son of God? I believe, and under again. Do you believe in the Holy Spirit, and the holy church? I believe. A third time. She comes up dripping, into a new life. Over time those questions grew into a statement many churches still say every week. A new part of the path begins here: what Christians believe. Today's word is the shape it comes in.
screen: `ROME, THE NIGHT BEFORE EASTER.` → `THREE QUESTIONS AT THE WATER.` → `I BELIEVE. I BELIEVE. I BELIEVE.`

segments.voice: Creed comes from the Latin credo, I believe, the creed's first word. Some language historians link credo to an old phrase meaning to put your heart on something. So believing isn't only agreeing with an idea; it's setting your heart on someone. In the West, the shorter creed is the Apostles' Creed. A lovely old legend says the twelve apostles each wrote one line of it, on the day of Pentecost. It isn't true; historians trace it to those baptism questions in Rome, slowly shaped over centuries. But it does carry the apostles' faith. In the English of the old prayer book it begins: "I believe in God the Father Almighty, Maker of heaven and earth." Then Jesus: born, suffered, crucified, died, buried, descended, rose, ascended, and coming again. Then the Holy Spirit, the church, the communion of saints, forgiveness, the resurrection of the body, the life everlasting. Early Christians called a creed a symbol, from the Greek symbolon, a token broken in two, whose halves fit together to prove who you were. Say the creed, and you show which family you belong to. Not every Christian uses creeds: Quakers keep no set creed, and some Baptists and Churches of Christ say they have no creed but the Bible, while holding much of the same faith. For two weeks, the path walks the creed one phrase a day, starting tomorrow with what it says first about God.

If you pray, go on with the creed's first line, I believe in God the Father Almighty, Maker of heaven and earth; if you don't, let the two words rest under your hand.

298.title: Maker of heaven and earth
298.hook: the world is made, meant and good (Genesis 1:31)
298.howItsDone: Christians say "Maker of heaven and earth" in the Apostles' and Nicene Creeds, give thanks for creation in grace before meals, and many churches keep a Season of Creation each autumn.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was creed: credo, I believe, and three questions at the water. Your line was a token broken in two.

A meal. A birthday card. A shelf that's only slightly crooked. A garden bed. Making something by hand often ends with a small moment: the maker steps back and looks. A breath out. That's good. Not perfect, maybe, but good, and theirs, and meant. The creed's very first sentence says that about everything. After I believe in God the Father Almighty comes: Maker of heaven and earth. And the Bible's first chapter ends with God stepping back to look at all of it: light and sea, trees and fish, animals and people. Today's word is that first line of the creed, and the first thing Christians say about the world.
screen: `SOMETHING YOU MADE.` → `STEPPING BACK: THAT'S GOOD.` → `THE CREED'S FIRST CLAIM.`

segments.voice: The Bible opens: "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth." The Hebrew verb for created is bara, and here's the surprise: when it means create, in the Bible, its subject is always God. People make, build, shape. Only God bara. Christians draw three things from this line. First, the world is made. It isn't an accident, and it isn't God. It's distinct from God, the way a song is distinct from the singer. Christian thinkers from the second century on said God made it out of nothing, not from material already lying around. Second, the world is meant. It has a purpose. It's here because someone wanted it to be. Third, the world is good. Six times in Genesis 1, God sees that what was made is good. The seventh time, looking at everything together, people included: "And God saw every thing that he had made, and, behold, it was very good." That mattered in the early church. Some teachers, often called Gnostics, taught that the material world was a mistake or a prison, and the body something to escape. The church said no. Matter, bodies, food, sex, earth, stars: made by God, and good. Christians today read Genesis in different ways alongside science. Some read the six days as literal days. Many churches, Catholic and many Protestant, see no conflict between creation and evolution: Genesis tells who and why, science tells how. They differ on how, but share the same first line. Made. Meant. Very good.
screen: `BARA: ONLY GOD CREATES.` · `MADE, NOT AN ACCIDENT.` · `MEANT, FOR A PURPOSE.` · `GOOD: THE BODY IS NO PRISON.` · then, large: `BEHOLD, IT WAS VERY GOOD.`

segments.voice: Look at something near you, a leaf, your own hand, a cup, the sky out the window, the way you'd look at something you'd made yourself: its color, its shape, how it works. Then quietly say: very good. If you pray, thank God, Maker of heaven and earth, for it; if you don't, just let yourself see it as good, and meant.
Bara. The Hebrew verb for create, used in the Bible only with God as its subject: the world made, meant, and very good.
Your line: very good. The seventh look, at everything together. Day two hundred ninety-eight, done.

299.title: One God, three persons
299.hook: Father, Son and Holy Spirit: one God in a communion of love
299.howItsDone: Many Christians make the sign of the cross "in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit," and many churches celebrate Trinity Sunday, the Sunday after Pentecost.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was bara: the world made, meant, and very good. Your line was very good.

In a Russian monastery, around six hundred years ago, a monk named Andrei Rublev painted an icon of God as Trinity. Three angels sit around a table, under a tree. It's the Genesis story of three visitors at Abraham's tent. They look almost identical, long-winged and gentle-faced, each head tilting toward the others. Nobody sits at the head of the table. Their hands and eyes make a circle. And at the front, facing you, there's an open place, as if someone has been invited in. Christians have looked at it for centuries to glimpse today's word.
screen: `RUBLEV'S ICON, AROUND 1420.` → `THREE AT ONE TABLE.` → `AN OPEN PLACE FACING YOU.`

segments.voice: Trinity comes from the Latin trinitas, a three-in-oneness. A North African writer named Tertullian used it around the year 200. Surprise: the word isn't in the Bible. The three names are, again and again. At Jesus's baptism: the Son in the water, the Spirit like a dove, the Father's voice from heaven. At the end of Matthew, Jesus sends his friends out, "baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost." Name, singular. Three, and one. Paul ends a letter with a blessing still said in churches: "The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Ghost, be with you all." Christians say the Trinity is one God in three persons: not three gods, and not one God wearing three masks. The councils spent decades finding words for it, and Christians are the first to call it a mystery. People try pictures, water as ice, liquid and steam, or a three-leaf shamrock, but theologians usually say every picture goes wrong somewhere. So why hold it at all? One answer starts from First John: God is love. Love needs someone to love, the reasoning goes. If God is Trinity, then before anything was made, God was already a communion: giving, receiving, sharing, forever. That's what Rublev painted: a circle of love, with a place left open. Some Christians, such as Unitarians, Jehovah's Witnesses and Latter-day Saints, understand God differently. For the Catholic, Orthodox and historic Protestant churches, the Trinity is at the center of the faith.
screen: `TRINITAS: NOT A BIBLE WORD.` · `THREE NAMES, ONE NAME.` · `A MYSTERY NO PICTURE HOLDS.` · `GOD IS LOVE, SO GOD IS COMMUNION.` · then, large: `THE COMMUNION OF THE HOLY GHOST.`

segments.voice: Think of three people who love each other, maybe you and two friends, a parent and two children, and picture them at one table. Notice how the love doesn't split into pieces; it goes round, and gets bigger with each person. If you pray, use Paul's blessing: the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Ghost. If you don't, rest in the picture of that table.
Trinity. Father, Son and Holy Spirit: one God, three persons, a communion of love.

300.title: The Word made flesh (John 1:14)
300.hook: God became human, born and hungry and tired
300.howItsDone: Christians celebrate the incarnation at Christmas, and in many churches people bow or kneel at the words "and was made man" in the Nicene Creed.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Trinity, and Rublev's table with a place left open. Your line was god is a communion.

Think about your body today. Maybe you woke up stiff. Maybe you were hungry by eleven. Maybe your feet hurt, or your eyes are tired from a screen, or you just need a nap. Ordinary, slightly embarrassing, completely human. Now here's a thought that has startled people for two thousand years. Christians say God knows exactly what that feels like. Not from a distance, like a doctor reading a chart. From the inside. God was once a baby who needed feeding in the night, a boy who scraped his knees, a man who walked until his feet were sore and sat down by a well, worn out. Today's word names it, in one short line from John's Gospel.
screen: `STIFF, HUNGRY, TIRED.` → `GOD KNOWS IT FROM THE INSIDE.` → `ONE SHORT LINE IN JOHN.`

segments.voice: Incarnation comes from Latin: in, plus caro, carnis, flesh. Same root as carnival and chili con carne. In-flesh-ment. John's Gospel begins with a poem about the Word, who was with God and was God, through whom everything was made. Then, in verse fourteen, the poem lands with a thud: "And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us." Flesh. John could have said body, or human nature. He chose the plainest, earthiest word there is. The Greek is sarx: meat, skin, the part of you that gets hungry and bleeds. And dwelt, in Greek, is literally pitched his tent. God camped among us. The Gospels don't flinch. Jesus is born and laid in a feeding trough. After forty days in the desert, Matthew says simply, he was hungry. In John, "Jesus therefore, being wearied with his journey, sat thus on the well." He sleeps through a storm in a boat. At his friend's grave, in the shortest verse in the King James Bible: "Jesus wept." Christians of every church see the incarnation as the center of the whole story, and Christmas is its feast. It means God didn't fix the world from outside. God came in. And your body, with its hunger and its tiredness, isn't beneath God. It was worth becoming. Early Christians put it this way: God took on everything human, so that everything human could be healed. Tomorrow, the other half: this tired man by the well was also, fully, God.

301.hook: the councils said: not half and half, but both at once
301.howItsDone: Christians confess Jesus as fully God and fully human in the Nicene Creed and in hymns, and many Orthodox Christians pray the Jesus Prayer, which names him Lord and Son of God.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was incarnation: the Word made flesh, hungry and tired by a well. Your line was the word became flesh.

Blue paint and yellow paint, stirred together, make green: something new, but no longer really blue or yellow. Tell a curious ten-year-old that Jesus is God and human, and that's often where the mind goes. So he's a mix? Half God, half human, like a hero from the old Greek myths? Or maybe he's really God, and the human part is a sort of costume. Or really a man, a very holy one, and God sort of lives in him. Someone in the early centuries taught a version of each, and each was turned down. Today's word is the answer the church gave instead, and it's stranger than any of them.
screen: `BLUE AND YELLOW MAKE GREEN.` → `HALF AND HALF? A COSTUME?` → `EVERY ONE TURNED DOWN.`

segments.voice: In 451, at Chalcedon, the council from day two hundred eighty-three, bishops wrote a careful statement. Christ, they said, is one person, fully God and fully human. Truly God, of one being with the Father. Truly human, with a body and a human mind and soul, like us in everything except sin. And the two natures are joined without being mixed, without being changed, without being divided, without being separated. Four withouts, and each one closes a door. Not mixed: he's not green paint. Not changed: God doesn't stop being God, and the human doesn't dissolve. Not divided or separated: he isn't two people sharing one body; he's one person, one who. Why did it matter? Recall yesterday's line, as a bishop named Gregory of Nazianzus put it, roughly: whatever of us he didn't take on, he didn't heal. If Jesus had no real human mind, our minds aren't healed. If he wasn't truly God, it isn't God who came close. The churches hold it as a mystery, not a puzzle to solve. The ancient churches of the east, from day two hundred eighty-four, put it in different words, one united nature, but they too say fully God and fully human. Look back at this week: Pentecostals and the Spirit; what the churches share; the creed; the Maker of heaven and earth; the Trinity; the Word made flesh; and today, both at once. A week on who God is, and who Jesus is.
